explanations.explanation: Fire it is. When Solomon, Israel's king, finishes praying, fire comes down from heaven and consumes the burnt offering and the sacrifices. Nobody lit that one with a match, friend. I've watched my oven for years and it has never once done that on its own.

Hail is a good guess if you're picturing something big falling from the sky. But the text says that after Solomon, Israel's king, finishes praying, fire comes down from heaven. It consumes the burnt offering and the sacrifices. Hail would just leave everything soggy, and I would NOT want to clean that up.

Manna did come from heaven once. God sent bread from the sky for Israel to gather in the wilderness (Exodus 16:4). But this scene is different. Here, after Solomon, Israel's king, finishes praying, fire comes down from heaven and consumes the burnt offering and the sacrifices.
Fills is right. The glory of the LORD filled the temple (2 Chronicles 7:1). That's the very moment the fire comes down and consumes the offerings. The very next verse shows how full it was.

No, nothing in the text has the glory leaving. It says the glory of the LORD filled the temple. The very next verse tells us the priests couldn't even get in because of it. That's about as far from leaving as you can get.

The text doesn't say a word about anything shaking. What it says is that the glory of the LORD filled the temple. The priests were unable to enter because the glory of the LORD had filled it (2 Chronicles 7:2). That's the full picture here, friend.

That's the opposite of what the text says. The priests were unable to enter the house of the LORD, because the glory of the LORD had filled it. They didn't walk in at all. The glory filling the house is what stopped them.

False is right. The text says the priests were unable to enter the house of the LORD, because the glory of the LORD had filled it. They couldn't go in, and that's the whole point of the verse. The glory of the LORD filled that house, friend.

explanations.answer: Bow with faces to the ground
explanations.explanation: They bowed down on the pavement with their faces to the ground. All the Israelites saw the fire coming down and the glory of the LORD above the temple, and down they went. Then they worshiped and gave thanks. Faces to the ground, friend, all of them.

explanations.answer: Run back toward the city gates
explanations.explanation: Running isn't what the text shows. It says that when all the Israelites saw the fire coming down and the glory of the LORD above the temple, they bowed down on the pavement with their faces to the ground. Then they worshiped and gave thanks to the LORD. I'd have been fumbling for the exit, friend, but the text has them bowing.

explanations.answer: Stand still and cover their eyes
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention anyone covering their eyes. It says they bowed down on the pavement with their faces to the ground, and they worshiped and gave thanks to the LORD. Bowing is what the text gives us. Faces down, friend.
Dedicated is right. The king and all the people dedicated the house of God. Notice that it's the king AND all the people, not just one man with a crown. That's a whole crowd of hands in one batch.

Rebuilt doesn't fit here. The text says the king and all the people dedicated the house of God, and nothing in this verse has anyone building. Back in 2 Chronicles 5:1, all the work Solomon did for the house of the LORD was finished. Dedicating is a different job, friend.

Nobody is pulling out a measuring tape here, friend. The text says the king and all the people dedicated the house of God. That's setting it apart for the LORD. I measure flour, but they were doing something much bigger.

King David made those instruments. The text says they were the instruments of the LORD, which King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD. It adds that David had offered praise with them, saying, “For His loving devotion endures forever.” Those words from David show up again in this very verse.

Saul? Friend, he's not in this verse at all, and I'm not letting him take the credit. The text says the instruments were the ones King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD. David had offered praise with them too. So this one goes to David.

SAMUEL?! Friend, you went straight for the big name, and I love the swagger. But he's not in this verse. The text says the instruments were the ones King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD (2 Chronicles 7:6). David made them, and David praised with them.
True. The priests sounded trumpets across from the Levites, and all the Israelites were standing. So the whole crowd is on its feet while the trumpets sound. That's a LOUD moment, friend.

The text says the opposite. Across from the Levites, the priests sounded trumpets, and all the Israelites were standing. Nobody was sitting this one out. Everyone is on their feet while the trumpets sound.

explanations.answer: The bronze altar can't hold them all
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. The bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold all these offerings. So he consecrated the middle of the courtyard in front of the house of the LORD, and offered them there. Too many offerings for the altar, so he used the courtyard.

explanations.answer: The bronze altar isn't finished yet
explanations.explanation: The text never says the altar is unfinished. It says Solomon had made the bronze altar, and it could not hold all these offerings. That's why he consecrated the middle of the courtyard. The problem was space, not construction.

explanations.answer: The crowd wants a closer look
explanations.explanation: A closer look? Friend, nobody's out there fighting for a front-row seat, and I'd bet nobody could see past those smoking offerings anyway. The text says the bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold all these offerings (2 Chronicles 7:7). So he consecrated the middle of the courtyard in front of the house of the LORD and offered them there.
Not quite, friend. The people didn't head straight home. The text says that on the eighth day they held a solemn assembly. Only after that did Solomon send them away, as verse 10 tells us.

False is right. The seven-day feast ends, but the text says that on the eighth day they held a solemn assembly. The dedication of the altar had lasted seven days, and the feast seven days more. So there's still one more gathering before anyone leaves.

That's right. Solomon sent the people away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart. The text says it was for the good things that the LORD had done for David, for Solomon, and for His people Israel. They left with their hearts full, and I think that's the best way to leave any gathering.

I'd be wiped out after all that, I'll admit. But the text doesn't say the people were tired. It says Solomon sent them away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart for the good things that the LORD had done. Joy is the word the text gives.

The text doesn't mention any worry. It says Solomon sent the people away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart. They were glad for the good things that the LORD had done for David, for Solomon, and for His people Israel. Joyful and glad is what the text gives us.
